Building terminal user interfaces: input events, screen and cursor control, colour.

Three builtins do what the language cannot otherwise reach — `set_raw_mode`,
`read_key`, `terminal_size` — and everything here is ordinary Lyra on top of them.
That split is the standard library's usual one: the syscall is primitive, the
interpretation is not.

Output needed no builtin at all, because `\e` reaches stdout as byte 27, so every
escape sequence in `screen.lyra`, `style.lyra` and `mouse.lyra` is just a string.
**Mouse input needed none either**, which is the surprising part: a terminal reports
clicks as escape sequences on stdin, so enabling it is a `print` and receiving it is
`read_key`.

## Examples

```lyra
set_raw_mode(true);
alt_screen_enter();
mouse_enable();
var events = event_reader();
var running = true;
while running {
  match events.next_event() {
    Some(Keyboard(Char c)) => { running = i64(c) != 113 },
    Some(Keyboard(Up)) => println("up"),
    Some(Mouse(m)) => println("click at ${m.col},${m.row}"),
    Some(_) => { },
    None => { running = false }
  }
}
mouse_disable();
alt_screen_leave();
set_raw_mode(false);
```

## Types

### `Event`

```lyra
pub data Event = Keyboard Key | Mouse MouseEvent
```

Something that happened at the terminal.

#### Members

- `Keyboard Key` — A keypress.
- `Mouse MouseEvent` — A mouse button, wheel notch or drag — only ever produced after `mouse_enable`.

### `EventReader`

```lyra
pub struct EventReader
```

A terminal input reader.

It exists to hold one code point of lookahead, which the Escape ambiguity forces:
recognizing `\e[A` means reading past the `\e`, and when what follows turns out *not*
to be a sequence, that key has already been consumed and has to go somewhere. Without
this it would simply be dropped.

#### Members

- `pending: Maybe<rune>` — A code point read while looking for an escape sequence and found not to be part of one. The next read takes it instead of going to the terminal.

### `Key`

```lyra
pub data Key = Char rune | Up | Down | Left | Right | Home | End | PageUp | PageDown | Delete | Enter | Tab | Backspace | Escape
```

A decoded keypress.

`Char` carries any key that is a character — including the ones a terminal sends as
control bytes but a reader thinks of as characters. The named constructors are the
keys that have no character to carry.

#### Examples

```lyra
var events = event_reader();
match events.next_event() {
  Some(Keyboard(Up)) => println("up"),
  Some(Keyboard(Char c)) => println("typed ${c}"),
  Some(_) => println("something else"),
  None => println("input ended")
}
```

#### Members

- `Char rune` — A character key, carrying its code point.
- `Up` — The up arrow.
- `Down` — The down arrow.
- `Left` — The left arrow.
- `Right` — The right arrow.
- `Home` — Home. The navigation keys are sent as `\e[H`/`\e[F` or as the numbered `\e[1~` family depending on the terminal — both spellings decode to these.
- `End` — End.
- `PageUp` — Page Up.
- `PageDown` — Page Down.
- `Delete` — The forward-delete key (`\e[3~`), not Backspace.
- `Enter` — Return/Enter, sent as CR in raw mode rather than the LF it is outside one.
- `Tab` — Tab.
- `Backspace` — Backspace — 127 (DEL) from nearly every terminal, or 8 (BS) from some.
- `Escape` — The Escape key itself. **Reported one keypress late** — see `next_event`.

### `MouseAction`

```lyra
pub data MouseAction = Press | Release | Move
```

What happened.

#### Members

- `Press` — A button went down, or the wheel turned a notch.
- `Release` — A button came up.
- `Move` — The pointer moved. Under `mouse_enable_motion` this arrives with a button held (a drag) or with `NoButton` (a bare move); `mouse_enable` alone never produces it.

### `MouseButton`

```lyra
pub data MouseButton = MouseLeft | MouseMiddle | MouseRight | WheelUp | WheelDown | NoButton
```

Which button an event is about.

#### Members

- `MouseLeft` — The left button.
- `MouseMiddle` — The middle button, or a pressed wheel.
- `MouseRight` — The right button.
- `WheelUp` — A wheel notch upward. Terminals report the wheel as a button press with no matching release, so a `WheelUp` is always a `Press` and never arrives in pairs.
- `WheelDown` — A wheel notch downward; a `Press` with no release, as `WheelUp` is.
- `NoButton` — Motion with nothing held down, reported only under `mouse_enable_motion`.

### `MouseEvent`

```lyra
pub struct MouseEvent
```

A mouse event, with the pointer's cell.

`col` and `row` are **0-based** — the top-left cell is `(0, 0)`, so a click indexes a
grid directly and `for x in 0..<width` compares against it without arithmetic.

The terminal's own numbering is 1-based, and that is exactly why the conversion
happens here: `mouse_event` subtracts the one and `move_to` adds it back, so the whole
library speaks the language's coordinates and only the two functions that touch an
escape sequence know the terminal's. The alternative puts a `- 1` at every call site
and gets it wrong at one of them.

#### Members

- `button: MouseButton` — The button, wheel notch, or `NoButton` for a bare move.
- `action: MouseAction` — Press, release, or motion.
- `col: i64` — Column, 0-based, counting from the left.
- `row: i64` — Row, 0-based, counting from the top.

### `Renderer`

```lyra
pub struct Renderer
```

A frame writer that remembers what is on the screen.

Construct one, hand each frame to `render`, and it writes the difference. It holds no
terminal state of its own — `alt_screen_enter`, `cursor_hide` and the rest are still the
caller's to pair — only the rows it last wrote.

#### Members

- `prev: []string` — The rows as last written to the screen. Empty means nothing is known to be there, so the next frame is written whole.
- `buf: []u8` — Scratch: the bytes of the frame being written, reused across frames.

  It lives here rather than in `render` because a local one is a fresh box, a fresh
  buffer and a growth realloc **per frame** — which is most of what a small frame costs.
  Cleared at the top of each render and refilled, so after the first frame the memory is
  already there and already big enough. It holds nothing between calls: `decode_utf8`
  copies out, so what is left here is capacity, not state.

## Functions

### `alt_screen_enter`

```lyra
pub let alt_screen_enter = () -> void
```

Switch to the alternate screen buffer: a blank screen that does not scroll, leaving
whatever the user had in their terminal untouched underneath.

This is what makes a full-screen program polite — on `alt_screen_leave` the shell's
scrollback comes back exactly as it was. Pair the two, and note that a program which
exits without leaving strands the user on a blank screen.

### `alt_screen_leave`

```lyra
pub let alt_screen_leave = () -> void
```

Return to the normal screen buffer, restoring what was on it before.

### `at`

```lyra
pub let at = pure (col: i64, row: i64) -> string
```

The escape sequence that puts the cursor at `col`, `row` — **0-based, column first**,
exactly as `move_to`, which is this printed.

The returning half exists because a diff has to compose positioning *into* the string
it prints once; `move_to` performs its sequence, which is right for placing a cursor and
useless for building a frame. It is the same split `style.lyra` and `screen.lyra` draw,
and the `+ 1`s that reconcile the terminal's 1-based numbering live here alone —
`move_to` is now `print(at(col, row))`.

### `bg`

```lyra
pub let bg = pure (color: i64) -> string
```

Background colour, from the same palette as `fg`.

### `bg_rgb`

```lyra
pub let bg_rgb = pure (r: i64, g: i64, b: i64) -> string
```

Background colour as 24-bit RGB, each component 0–255. See `fg_rgb` for the range
hazard and the support caveat.

### `bold`

```lyra
pub let bold = pure () -> string
```

Bold, or on many terminals simply brighter.

### `box_bottom`

```lyra
pub let box_bottom = pure (width: i64) -> string
```

The bottom edge: `└───────┘`. Traps on a width under 2, as `box_top` does.

### `box_row`

```lyra
pub let box_row = pure (text: string, width: i64) -> string
```

A content row: `│ text  │`, the text fitted to the space between the borders.

The text is `fit` to `width - 2`, so it is cut when long and padded when short and the
right border always lands in the same column. An escape sequence inside `text` breaks
that, exactly as it breaks `fit` — it occupies no columns while counting as runes — so
colour goes *around* the whole row rather than inside it.

#### Panics
Traps on a width under 2, as `box_top` does.

### `box_top`

```lyra
pub let box_top = pure (width: i64) -> string
```

The top edge: `┌───────┐` at exactly `width` columns.

#### Panics
Traps if `width` is less than 2, which cannot hold the two corners. Unlike `fit`, there
is no smaller box to return — the borders *are* the box, so a width that cannot hold
them is a wrong call rather than a tight one, and a layout that computed it will not be
improved by silently drawing something else. Nearly every real width here is a constant
or comes from `terminal_size()`, which answers 80x24 rather than something degenerate
when there is no window.

### `box_top_titled`

```lyra
pub let box_top_titled = pure (title: string, width: i64) -> string
```

A top edge carrying a title: `┌─ Title ────┐`.

The title is cut to whatever room is left after the corners, the two rule characters
that frame it and its two spaces, so a long title shortens the rule to nothing rather
than pushing the corner off the row. That is the `fit` rule applied to a smaller
interior, and it is why the width arithmetic is worth having in one place.

#### Panics
Traps on a width under 2, as `box_top` does.

### `clear`

```lyra
pub let clear = () -> void
```

Erase the whole screen. Does not move the cursor — pair with `cursor_home` (or
`move_to`) unless the next thing written positions itself.

### `clear_line`

```lyra
pub let clear_line = () -> void
```

Erase from the cursor to the end of the line.

Redrawing a status bar with this is what stops a shorter line leaving the tail of the
longer one that was there before, which is the classic flicker-free-redraw bug.

### `cursor_hide`

```lyra
pub let cursor_hide = () -> void
```

Hide the cursor. Worth doing for the duration of a full-screen redraw: a visible
cursor skitters across the screen as the frame is written.

### `cursor_home`

```lyra
pub let cursor_home = () -> void
```

Move the cursor to the top-left corner.

### `cursor_show`

```lyra
pub let cursor_show = () -> void
```

Show the cursor again. A program that hides it and exits leaves the user with no
cursor in their shell, so this pairs with `cursor_hide` the way `alt_screen_leave`
pairs with `alt_screen_enter`.

### `digit_value`

```lyra
pub let digit_value = pure noalloc (c: rune) -> i64
```

The value of an ASCII decimal digit, 0..9.

#### Panics

Never traps, but answers nonsense for a non-digit — guard with `is_digit`, as the
sequence readers do. The conversion to i64 is the one thing a rune literal cannot
express: subtracting `'0'` is arithmetic, and arithmetic on runes is not a thing this
language offers.

### `dim`

```lyra
pub let dim = pure () -> string
```

Dim/faint. Not universally supported; degrades to ordinary text.

### `event_reader`

```lyra
pub let event_reader = pure () -> EventReader
```

A fresh reader with nothing buffered.

### `fg`

```lyra
pub let fg = pure (color: i64) -> string
```

Foreground colour, from the 256-colour palette.

0–7 are the basic colours, 8–15 their bright variants, 16–231 a 6×6×6 RGB cube, and
232–255 a 24-step grey ramp. `grey` and `rgb` below build the last two, which are the
two worth computing rather than memorizing.

#### Panics

Never traps; a number outside 0–255 produces a sequence the terminal ignores.

### `fg_rgb`

```lyra
pub let fg_rgb = pure (r: i64, g: i64, b: i64) -> string
```

Foreground colour as **24-bit RGB**, each component 0–255.

#### Beware the range

`rgb` takes 0–5 and this takes 0–255, and the two are one letter apart at the call
site. `fg(rgb(5, 0, 0))` and `fg_rgb(5, 0, 0)` are both valid and the second is almost
black — the mistake produces a picture, not an error, which is why the range is the
first thing said about each.

#### Support

Not universal. Every terminal supports the 256-colour palette `fg`/`bg` use; 24-bit
colour is widespread but not guaranteed — iTerm2, Ghostty, WezTerm, Kitty and Alacritty
have it, macOS's own Terminal.app does not, and there a program using this renders its
escape sequences as visible text. There is no way to ask the terminal, so this is the
caller's choice to make, not something the library can decide.

It also costs bytes: up to 19 per cell against 11 for the palette form, which matters
for a full-screen redraw where every byte is parsed by the terminal.

#### Examples

```lyra
print(fg_rgb(255, 128, 0) ++ "orange" ++ reset())
```

### `fit`

```lyra
pub let fit = pure (text: string, width: i64) -> string
```

`text` at exactly `width` columns: cut if long, padded with spaces if short.

#### Examples

```lyra
print(fit(" generation ${n} · q quits ", cols))
```

**The cut is the half that prevents a bug rather than a blemish.** A terminal has no
notion of a line too wide — it wraps onto the next row, and wrapping off the *last* row
scrolls the whole screen, so every cell of the frame is then displayed one row above
where it was written. A full-screen program with a status bar reads that as the display
jittering; one that also handles the mouse reads it as clicks toggling the wrong cell,
since the pointer still reports true screen rows. Each wrapped line shifts it by one.

**The padding is the other half.** A status line redrawn without `clear_line` leaves
the tail of whatever longer line was there before, so a short string must arrive at
full width rather than merely not too wide.

A rune is not always one column — a wide CJK glyph occupies two — so this is exact for
the text a status bar is usually made of and an over-estimate of the room left by
anything wider. Correcting it needs a character-width table, which is a larger feature
than this file.

### `grey`

```lyra
pub let grey = pure (level: i64) -> i64
```

The palette index for one of the 24 greys, `level` from 0 (near black) to 23 (near
white). Clamped, on `rgb`'s reasoning.

The ramp excludes true black and true white; those are palette 16 and 231, reachable
through `rgb(0, 0, 0)` and `rgb(5, 5, 5)`.

### `inverse`

```lyra
pub let inverse = pure () -> string
```

Swap foreground and background. The portable way to highlight a selected row, since
it needs no assumption about what the user's colours are.

### `is_digit`

```lyra
pub let is_digit = pure noalloc (c: rune) -> bool
```

Whether a code point is an ASCII decimal digit.

### `mouse_disable`

```lyra
pub let mouse_disable = () -> void
```

Stop reporting the mouse, whichever of the two enables was used.

Disabling a mode that was never enabled is harmless, so this needs no memory of which
one was.

### `mouse_enable`

```lyra
pub let mouse_enable = () -> void
```

Report button presses, releases and wheel notches.

**Pair this with `mouse_disable`**, exactly as `alt_screen_enter` pairs with
`alt_screen_leave` — a program that exits without disabling leaves the terminal
emitting escape sequences into the user's shell, where they arrive as garbage text on
every click.

### `mouse_enable_motion`

```lyra
pub let mouse_enable_motion = () -> void
```

As `mouse_enable`, and also report motion while a button is held (a drag).

Kept separate rather than made the default because it is *much* noisier: a drag across
the screen produces an event per cell entered, where a click produces two. Enable it
when a drag is what the program is for, not routinely.

### `move_to`

```lyra
pub let move_to = (col: i64, row: i64) -> void
```

Move the cursor to `col`, `row` — **0-based, and column first**.

The width-first order matches `terminal_size()` and every other pair in this library,
and is the reverse of the escape sequence underneath, which is `\e[<row>;<col>H`. One
place has to flip, and it is better that it be this line than every call site.

**0-based on the same reasoning**, which is the argument the line above already makes
applied to the origin rather than the order. The terminal counts from one — `\e[1;1H`
is the top-left cell — and the `+ 1` that reconciles it lives in `at` (frame.lyra),
paired with the `- 1` in `mouse_event`. Everything else in Lyra indexes from zero, so a
coordinate that came from a click lands in `grid[row][col]` with no arithmetic and a
loop written `0..<rows` compares against it directly. Hiding the terminal's numbering is
what this library is for; a program that hand-checks an escape sequence is reading this
line.

This *is* `at`, printed: a frame diff has to compose the same sequence into a string
rather than perform it, and one of the two had to be written in terms of the other or
the arithmetic would exist twice.

### `renderer`

```lyra
pub let renderer = pure () -> Renderer
```

A renderer that assumes nothing is on the screen, so the first frame is written whole.

### `reset`

```lyra
pub let reset = pure () -> string
```

Reset every attribute — colour, bold, the lot.

**Emit this at the end of anything styled.** A colour is terminal state, not a
property of the string that set it, so an unreset colour runs on into whatever is
printed next, including the user's shell prompt after the program exits.

### `rgb`

```lyra
pub let rgb = pure (r: i64, g: i64, b: i64) -> i64
```

The palette index for a point in the 6×6×6 RGB cube, each component 0–5.

Components are **clamped rather than trapped**, which is the opposite of what this
language does with an out-of-range index and is deliberate: a colour is decoration,
and a program computing one from a value it is visualizing should not die at the edge
of its own gradient. Getting a slightly wrong shade is the appropriate failure.

#### Examples

```lyra
print(fg(rgb(5, 0, 0)) ++ "red" ++ reset())
```

### `status_bar`

```lyra
pub let status_bar = pure (text: string, cols: i64) -> string
```

`text` as a full-width status row.

```lyra
rows.push(status_bar("${count} items · q quits", cols))
```

**Full width is the point, not the styling.** A bar redrawn shorter than the one before
leaves the tail of the old one on screen, and an inverse bar makes that obvious — the
stale text is inverted too. `fit` pads, so the row always covers the whole line.

The trailing `reset` closes the inversion, so the row composes into a frame without
tinting whatever follows it.

### `status_split`

```lyra
pub let status_split = pure (left: string, right: string, cols: i64) -> string
```

A status row with `left` at the left edge and `right` at the right, padded between.

```lyra
rows.push(status_split(path, "${row}:${col}", cols))
```

**The right segment wins when there is not room for both.** It is the one that changes
— a position, a count, a clock — and a reader tracking it needs it in a fixed place;
the left is usually a name, which reads fine truncated. So `left` is cut to whatever is
left over, and only if `right` alone overflows the row is *it* cut.

## Methods on `EventReader`

### `event_available`

```lyra
pub let event_available = (self: EventReader, timeout_ms: i64) -> bool
```

Whether an event is ready to be read, waiting up to `timeout_ms` for one.

This is what lets a program do something *other* than wait for input — redraw on a
resize, animate, poll a clock — instead of blocking in `next_event` until a key
arrives.

It consults the lookahead buffer first, which a bare `wait_for_key_ms` cannot: a code
point already read and held here is an event that is ready even though the terminal
has nothing new to offer.

**True does not promise a key.** At end of input this answers true and the
`next_event` that follows answers `None` — which is the whole reason the underlying
builtin is a bool rather than a timed read returning `Maybe`: the two outcomes stay
distinguishable instead of collapsing into one `None`.

### `next_event`

```lyra
pub let next_event = (self: mut EventReader) -> Maybe<Event>
```

The next event, or `None` once input has ended.

#### Panics

Never traps. `None` is the end of input, exactly as it is for `read_key`.

**A lone Escape is reported immediately** as of 08/17. `\e` begins every arrow,
navigation key and mouse report, so on reading one this must look at what follows to
know what it has — and with only a blocking read that meant waiting for the user's
*next* keypress, so Escape arrived one key late. `wait_for_key_ms` resolves it: if
nothing follows the `\e` within `escape_timeout_ms`, it was the Escape key.

The lookahead buffer is still needed and still does its job — a key that follows an
Escape too quickly to be a timeout is read, found not to be a sequence introducer, and
handed back on the next call rather than dropped.

## Methods on `Renderer`

### `invalidate`

```lyra
pub let invalidate = (self: mut Renderer) -> void
```

Forget what is on the screen, so the next `render` writes the whole frame.

Needed after anything that changes the screen behind the renderer's back — `clear()`,
leaving and re-entering the alternate buffer, and above all a **resize**, where the
terminal reflows what was there and the remembered rows no longer describe it. A
program that redraws on `terminal_size` changing should call this in the same branch.

### `render`

```lyra
pub let render = (self: mut Renderer, rows: []string) -> void
```

Write the rows that differ from the previous frame, in one `print`.

```lyra
var r = renderer()
for _ in 0..<frames {
  var rows: []string = []
  for y in 0..<rows_count { rows.push(paint_row(y, cols)) }
  rows.push(status_bar("q quits", cols))
  r.render(rows)
}
```

**Consecutive changed rows share one cursor move.** The measurement this library is
built on is that positioning per cell costs more than the text does; positioning per
*row* is the same mistake one order of magnitude down, and a frame where the top half
scrolls would pay it on every row. A run of adjacent changed rows is written as one
position escape followed by the rows joined with `\r\n`, so the common cases — one row
changed, or a contiguous band — cost one move each.

**Every row must be the full width of the screen.** A row shorter than the one it
replaces leaves the tail of the old one on screen, which is `fit`'s reason for
existing. This deliberately does *not* append an erase-to-end-of-line: that erases with
the **current background colour**, so on a row that ends inside a coloured span it
paints the rest of the line in that colour — a worse artifact than the one it fixes,
and one that appears only on the frames where colour is used.

#### Panics
Never traps. A frame with more or fewer rows than the last is handled by writing the
rows that are new; see `invalidate` for what a *resize* needs on top of that.
